Now let's think about what this means when you lay out a row of blocks inside a chunk.

**The problem that alignment creates inside a chunk**

Imagine you have a chunk of raw memory starting at address 0, and your block size is 48 bytes. Block 0 starts at address 0, block 1 starts at address 48, block 2 starts at address 96, block 3 starts at address 144. Each block's starting address is just the previous one plus 48.

Now suppose the objects that will live in these blocks require 16-byte alignment. Is every block's starting address a multiple of 16? Block 0 is at 0 — yes. Block 1 is at 48 — yes (48 = 16 × 3). Block 2 is at 96 — yes (96 = 16 × 6). Block 3 is at 144 — yes (144 = 16 × 9). This works out because 48 happens to be a multiple of 16.

Now change the block size to 50 bytes. Block 0 is at 0, block 1 is at 50, block 2 is at 100, block 3 is at 150. Is 50 a multiple of 16? No. Is 100? No. Is 150? No. So blocks 1, 2, and 3 are all misaligned. The object inside block 1 requires an address that's a multiple of 16, but it's sitting at address 50, which isn't one.

This is the core problem. When you lay blocks out contiguously — each one immediately after the previous — the starting address of every block after the first is determined by the block size. If the block size is a multiple of the alignment, every block lands on an aligned address. If it isn't, most of them won't.

The fix is straightforward: you pad the block size up to the nearest multiple of the alignment. A 50-byte object with 16-byte alignment gets a 64-byte block (the next multiple of 16 after 50). You're wasting 14 bytes per block, but every block is now guaranteed to land on an aligned address when blocks are placed contiguously. That's internal fragmentation — the same concept from section 1, now showing up because of alignment rather than allocator bookkeeping.

On x86-64 Linux, the fundamental type with the strictest alignment is typically `long double` or certain SIMD-related types, and that alignment is 16 bytes. `max_align_t` is a type defined by the C++ standard whose alignment *is* that strictest fundamental alignment for your platform.

The practical meaning is simple: if your blocks are aligned to `alignof(max_align_t)` — which is 16 on x86-64 — then any standard C++ type can be placed in your block without alignment issues. `int`, `double`, `uint64_t`, pointers — they all require 16 or less. Here's where your intuition was heading in the right direction. When you call `malloc` to get a chunk of memory, you get back a pointer. You don't get to choose what address that pointer points to. `malloc` *does* guarantee that the returned address is suitably aligned for any fundamental type — meaning it's aligned to `max_align_t`, so on x86-64 you're guaranteed a 16-byte-aligned address. But that's a guarantee of the standard, not something you asked for.

So if 16-byte alignment is all you need for your blocks, `malloc` has you covered. You get a chunk starting at, say, address 1024 (a multiple of 16), your block size is a multiple of 16, and every block within the chunk lands on a multiple of 16. No extra work.

These functions do whatever internal work is necessary — possibly requesting extra memory from the OS and then adjusting the pointer forward to hit the right boundary — so you don't have to.

Your instinct was exactly right: without these functions, you'd have to manually over-allocate and adjust the pointer yourself. Request more memory than you need from `malloc`, then manually advance the pointer to the next aligned address within that allocation. So if you acquire chunks via `mmap`, alignment is guaranteed to be more than sufficient for any block alignment requirement.

**Your question about block sizes at the process level**

You asked whether it makes sense for process-level blocks to be cache-line-sized, and the honest answer is: no, probably not.

Your process-wide pool is the root of the hierarchy. It's handing out blocks to downstream components, and those blocks are being subdivided further. These are large blocks — probably kilobytes or more — that serve as arenas or sub-pools for downstream work. A 64-byte cache-line-sized block at this level would be far too small to serve as the raw material for a downstream allocator.

Cache line alignment at the process level *does* still matter, but in a different way. You want the *start* of each large block to be cache-line-aligned (or at least well-aligned) so that the downstream component receiving that block can build its own aligned structures on top of it without worrying about the starting address being awkward. But the block size itself should reflect the granularity of distribution in your hierarchy — how much memory each downstream component needs — not the CPU cache line size.

Put differently: at the root, your alignment concern is about giving downstream components a clean starting address. At the leaves of your hierarchy, where small objects are being allocated and accessed by individual threads, that's where cache-line-sized blocks and false sharing prevention become directly relevant. Each level of the hierarchy has its own alignment considerations appropriate to its scope.

For your process-wide pool, rounding block sizes up to a multiple of 64 (the cache line size) ensures that every block starts on a cache line boundary, which gives downstream components the cleanest possible foundation. But the blocks themselves might be 4KB, 16KB, 64KB — whatever your hierarchy needs.

Exactly right, and the reasoning is precisely what you described. If you're writing cross-platform code, `std::aligned_alloc` from C++17 is the cleanest choice because it works everywhere without `#ifdef` blocks. Just note that memory from `std::aligned_alloc` is freed with `std::free`, same as `malloc`.

Let's get into thread safety.

---

**Why thread safety is a problem for pools**

Your pool is process-wide. Multiple threads will call allocate and deallocate concurrently. If two threads try to pop the head of the free list at the same time without any coordination, they can both read the same head pointer, both think they're getting different blocks, and both walk away with the same block. One of them writes their data, the other overwrites it. Corruption.

The free list is the critical shared state. Every allocate reads and modifies the head pointer. Every deallocate reads and modifies the head pointer. If those operations aren't atomic with respect to each other, the list gets torn — pointers end up stale, blocks get lost, blocks get double-handed-out. This is the same class of problem you studied with your lock-free deque work, just in a simpler data structure.

There are three broad approaches to making this safe, and they sit on a spectrum from simple-and-slow to complex-and-fast.

**Approach 1: A single global mutex**

The simplest solution. You protect the entire pool with one mutex. Every allocate locks the mutex, pops the head, unlocks. Every deallocate locks the mutex, pushes onto the head, unlocks. Correctness is trivial — only one thread can touch the free list at a time.

The problem is contention. If you have 16 threads all allocating heavily, 15 of them are waiting at any given moment. The mutex becomes a serialization point. Under light load this is fine — the critical section is tiny (a pointer read, a pointer write, done), so the lock is held for nanoseconds. But under heavy concurrent allocation, those nanoseconds compound because of the cost of the lock itself: the atomic operations involved in acquiring and releasing the mutex, potential context switches if the lock is contended, and cache line bouncing as the mutex's state moves between cores.

For a pool where allocation is infrequent relative to the work done with each block, a global mutex is perfectly acceptable. If your downstream components grab a large block and use it for a long time before returning it, the lock is rarely contended and the simplicity is worth it.

**Approach 2: Per-thread caching with a shared backing pool**

This is the pattern that Bonwick and Adams introduced in the Magazines paper, and it's what `tcmalloc` (thread-caching malloc) is named after. The idea is to give each thread its own small private cache of blocks that it can allocate from and deallocate to without any synchronization at all. When a thread's local cache is empty, it goes to the shared pool and grabs a batch of blocks under a lock, refilling its cache. When its local cache is full (too many freed blocks accumulating), it returns a batch to the shared pool.

The lock still exists on the shared pool, but it's hit far less frequently. Instead of locking on every single allocation, a thread locks once to grab, say, 32 blocks, then satisfies the next 31 allocations purely from its local cache with no locking, no atomics, no contention. The amortized cost of synchronization drops by a factor of the batch size.

This is a layered design — the per-thread cache is a fast path, and the shared pool is the slow path. Most allocations hit the fast path. The slow path exists for replenishment and for balancing memory across threads that have different allocation rates.

The tradeoff is complexity and memory overhead. Each thread holds some blocks in its local cache that are technically free from the pool's perspective but unavailable to other threads. If you have 16 threads each caching 32 blocks, that's 512 blocks sitting in local caches that might never be used if those threads aren't actively allocating. For a pool with a fixed memory ceiling, this reserved-but-idle memory eats into your budget.

There's also the question of what happens when a thread dies. Its local cache holds blocks that need to be returned to the shared pool. You need a cleanup mechanism — thread-local storage destructors, or explicit deregistration — to reclaim those blocks.

**Approach 3: Lock-free free list**

You can make the free list itself lock-free using compare-and-swap (CAS) operations. The idea is straightforward given your atomics background. To allocate, you read the current head, read the next pointer from the block at that head, then do a CAS on the head pointer — "if the head is still what I read, swap it to the next pointer." If another thread modified the head between your read and your CAS, the CAS fails and you retry.

Deallocation works the same way in reverse. You write the current head into the block being returned as its next pointer, then CAS the pool's head — "if the head is still what I read, swap it to this returned block." Retry on failure.

This eliminates the mutex entirely. No thread ever blocks — they either succeed or retry. Under low contention, the CAS almost always succeeds on the first try and the cost is essentially a single atomic operation per allocate or deallocate. Under high contention, threads spin-retry, which wastes CPU but doesn't cause the context-switch overhead of a mutex.

You'll recognize a risk here from your atomics studies: the ABA problem. Thread 1 reads head as block A. Thread 2 allocates block A, does some work, frees block A — it's back at the head. Thread 1's CAS sees "head is still A" and succeeds, but the list structure may have changed underneath. In a singly-linked free list where blocks are interchangeable, ABA is actually less dangerous than in a general lock-free data structure, because the pool doesn't care *which* block it hands out — any free block is as good as any other. But it can still cause issues if the next pointer inside block A was changed between thread 1's read and its CAS. The classic solution is a tagged pointer — pairing the head pointer with a monotonically increasing counter so the CAS checks both the pointer and the counter, detecting any intervening modifications even if the pointer value returns to its original state.

**What makes sense for your design**

Given what you've described — a process-wide pool handing out large blocks to downstream components — the allocation rate at this level is probably not extreme. Downstream components grab a block, use it for a significant scope of work, then return it. This isn't a hot loop where millions of tiny allocations happen per second. It's more like a resource checkout and return pattern.

That access pattern points toward approach 1 (global mutex) as the right starting point. The critical section is tiny, the contention will be low because allocations are infrequent relative to block lifetimes, and the simplicity keeps your implementation clean while you build the rest of the hierarchy. The downstream components — the ones doing high-frequency small allocations within their blocks — are where per-thread caching or lock-free techniques would pay off, because that's where the hot paths live.

If profiling later shows the mutex is actually a bottleneck, you can drop in a lock-free free list without changing the pool's external API. But starting with a mutex gives you correct, debuggable, simple code, and for large-block low-frequency allocation it's likely sufficient for the lifetime of the project.

**The memory ordering connection**

One last point that ties back to your atomics and memory model work. Whichever approach you use, the synchronization has to establish the right happens-before relationships. When thread A frees a block and thread B subsequently allocates that same block, thread B must see everything thread A wrote into it before freeing it — otherwise thread B is reading stale or partially-written data. A mutex provides this automatically (unlock happens-before the next lock). A CAS with `memory_order_acq_rel` provides it in the lock-free case — the releasing thread's CAS publishes its writes, and the acquiring thread's CAS observes them. This is exactly the release/acquire semantics you studied, applied directly.

That's the thread safety landscape. The three approaches form a progression: mutex for simplicity when contention is low, per-thread caching for throughput when contention is moderate, and lock-free for maximum concurrency when every nanosecond matters. For your root pool, the simple end of that spectrum is where you belong. The complexity lives further down your hierarchy.

That's a sound engineering call — designing for the worst case when you can't control the usage patterns is the right posture for a library.

The Bonwick and Adams paper is the same one I mentioned in the reading list earlier — "Magazines and Vmem: Extending the Slab Allocator to Many CPUs and Arbitrary Resources," presented at USENIX Annual Technical Conference in 2001. The PDF is available directly from USENIX at `usenix.org/publications/library/proceedings/usenix01/full_papers/bonwick/bonwick.pdf`. It covers the magazine layer in detail — how per-CPU caches are structured, how magazines (pre-filled arrays of pointers to free objects) get swapped in and out of the caches, and how the whole thing layers on top of the slab allocator from the 1994 paper. Given your decision to go lock-free, pay particular attention to how they batch objects between the local and global layers — that batching concept translates directly to a lock-free design where you'd use CAS to move batches between a thread-local cache and the shared pool atomically.

Let's close this out with section 7.

---

**What the downstream interface actually needs to accomplish**

Your pool is the root of a hierarchy. It owns a capped region of memory, carves it into large blocks, and hands those blocks to downstream components. Those components build their own allocation strategies — sub-pools, arenas, whatever — on top of the blocks they receive. The interface between your pool and those downstream consumers is a contract, and the design of that contract determines how robust, misuse-resistant, and flexible the whole hierarchy is.

There are three concerns: how consumers get blocks, how they return blocks, and how you prevent them from corrupting the pool's internal state.

**Acquisition — how a block is handed out**

The simplest interface is a function that returns a pointer to a raw block of memory. Something conceptually like `void* allocate()` — the caller gets a pointer, the block size is fixed and known, and the caller can do whatever they want with those bytes.

But "a raw pointer to some bytes" is a very thin contract. The caller has to know the block size externally. There's no type information. There's no way to associate metadata with the block without the caller managing that themselves. And when it comes time to return the block, the caller just hands back a raw pointer and you have to trust it.

A richer approach is to return a handle or a wrapper type instead of a raw pointer. This could be as simple as a small struct that contains the pointer and the block size, or it could be a more opaque handle — an index into an internal table — that the caller uses to refer to the block without ever touching the pointer directly. The handle approach gives you a layer of indirection that enables validation, tracking, and prevents callers from forging or corrupting block references.

However, a handle-based interface adds overhead and indirection, and for a performance-critical library, that cost may not be justified. The right choice depends on how much you trust downstream code. If the downstream components are also part of your library — internal layers of the hierarchy that you control — raw pointers are fine because you're writing both sides. If external user code can interact with the pool directly, a handle provides safety. You can also offer both: a raw fast path for internal use and a safe wrapper for external use.

**Return — how a block comes back**

Deallocation is where misuse causes the most damage. The dangers are: returning a pointer that didn't come from this pool, returning the same block twice (double free), and using a block after returning it (use-after-free).

Double free is particularly insidious with an embedded free list. If a block is already in the free list and you push it onto the head again, you create a cycle — the block points to some other free block, and that other block (or some chain eventually) points back to this one. The next two allocations will hand out the same block to two different callers. Silent corruption.

For a lock-free pool in a generic library, you have to decide how much defensive checking to include. There are several options with different cost profiles.

You could do no validation at all, which gives maximum speed but means any misuse silently corrupts the pool. This is what most high-performance allocators do — they document the contract and trust the caller.

You could add a debug mode with validation — a compile-time flag that enables checks like verifying the pointer falls within a known chunk, or checking a canary value placed at the start or end of each block that should be intact when the block is returned. This adds overhead only when debugging is enabled.

You could use a poisoning pattern — when a block is freed, you fill it with a known byte pattern (like 0xDEADBEEF repeated). If you later allocate that block and the pattern is intact, the block wasn't written to after being freed. If someone reads a freed block and sees the poison pattern, they know they're hitting use-after-free. This is a diagnostic aid, not a prevention mechanism, but it makes bugs visible rather than silent.

**Preventing pool corruption from the outside**

The fundamental rule is: callers should never be able to reach the pool's internal state. The free list head pointer, the chunk list, the growth logic — none of this should be accessible through the public interface. The only operations a caller can perform are "give me a block" and "here's a block back." Everything else is private.

This sounds obvious, but it has a specific implication for embedded free lists. Remember that the next-pointer in a free block is stored in the block's own bytes. When you hand that block to a caller, the caller overwrites those bytes with their own data — that's fine, the block is allocated, the next-pointer is gone. But when the block comes back and you push it onto the free list, you write a next-pointer into it. If the caller retains a reference to the block and continues reading from it, they'll see your free-list pointer where their data used to be. This is use-after-free on the caller's side, and it's their bug, but it does mean your internal structure (the address of the next free block) is technically visible to buggy caller code.

In a debug build, poisoning the rest of the block on free (everything after the next-pointer) can help surface this. In a release build, you accept that the caller's contract is "don't touch the block after returning it" and move on.

**The ownership model**

For your hierarchy specifically, the ownership model needs to be clear across levels. When the root pool hands a block to a downstream component, that component *owns* the block until it explicitly returns it. The root pool must not reclaim, reuse, or inspect that block while it's owned by someone else. The downstream component may subdivide the block internally however it wants — it could run an arena, a sub-pool, or hand raw slices to application code — but it is responsible for ensuring that all its internal users are done with the block before returning it to the root pool.

This means teardown in your hierarchy has to be bottom-up. The lowest-level consumers release their resources first, then the mid-level components return their blocks to the root pool, and finally the root pool releases its chunks back to the OS. If any level returns a block while a lower level is still using memory within it, you get use-after-free across hierarchy boundaries — the most dangerous kind, because the corruption might not manifest until much later.

Your systematic teardown at process exit handles this naturally, but the ownership contract should still be explicit in the API so that any future runtime deallocation (if you ever add it) follows the same discipline.

Keeping it minimal, your pool's public interface likely has four elements. Construction, where you specify the block size, alignment, and memory ceiling. An allocate function that returns a block or signals exhaustion. A deallocate function that takes a block back. And destruction, which releases everything to the OS.

Everything else — growth, free list management, chunk tracking, thread-local caching — is internal. The downstream components interact with the pool through those four operations and nothing more. The cleaner this boundary is, the easier it is to change the pool's internals (swapping a mutex for a CAS, changing the growth strategy, adding debug instrumentation) without affecting any downstream code.

---

That's the full arc — from why pools exist, through the vocabulary, the mechanical core, growth, alignment, thread safety, and finally the interface contract. Once that's solid, layer the CAS-based free list on top. Then add the per-thread caching. Each layer is a clean addition that doesn't restructure what's below it.

Alright, let me think through this carefully because there's a real question of whether this layering earns its keep.

**What you're describing with `MemoryCore`**

You see `MemoryCore` as an orchestrator — it doesn't just hold a pool, it coordinates multiple memory-related concerns at the process level. The pool is one of those concerns (general block distribution to downstream components). Infrastructure memory is potentially another (dedicated memory for Chevron's own internal machinery). And a memory allocator component might be a third (though that one is the vaguest of the three). `MemoryCore` would present a unified interface over these composed parts, and downstream code would interact with `MemoryCore` rather than reaching into any individual component.

**Where I think this idea has merit**

The separation between `ProcessMemoryPool` and `MemoryCore` makes sense if `MemoryCore` genuinely has orchestration work to do that doesn't belong inside the pool itself. The pool's job is mechanical — hold blocks, hand them out, take them back. If there are process-level memory concerns that sit *above* that mechanical job, they need a home, and stuffing them into the pool would violate the pool's focused responsibility.

The OS negotiation point is a real one. Deciding *when* to acquire memory, *how much* to acquire, and enforcing the budget ceiling are policy decisions. The pool is the mechanism — it holds and distributes what it's given. `MemoryCore` could be the policy — it decides when to tell the pool to grow, tracks how much of the ceiling has been consumed, and refuses requests that would exceed the budget. That's a clean separation: `MemoryCore` owns the budget and the acquisition strategy, `ProcessMemoryPool` owns the blocks and the free list.

**Where I have concerns**

The infrastructure memory idea is the one I want to push on. You're imagining that Chevron's own internal components — per-window infrastructure, subsystem state, whatever the library needs for itself — might get their memory from a separate managed region rather than from the general pool. The motivation would be keeping library infrastructure memory distinct from user-facing memory, potentially with different lifecycle or layout characteristics.

Here's my honest take: this separation is only justified if Chevron infrastructure memory has genuinely different *mechanical* requirements from general memory. If infrastructure objects are allocated once during setup and freed once during teardown — long-lived, low-churn — then they have a fundamentally different allocation pattern from downstream scope memory that might be allocated and freed rapidly during runtime. Different patterns can justify different strategies. An arena for infrastructure (bump allocate during init, bulk free at teardown) versus a pool for general distribution would be a legitimate split.

But if infrastructure memory just needs blocks from the same pool, allocated and freed in the same way, with the same lifetime characteristics, then carving out a separate region for it adds complexity without buying you anything. You'd be managing two sources of blocks with identical mechanics just because the *consumer* is different, which isn't a strong enough reason.

I'd say defer the infrastructure memory question until you have a concrete inventory of what Chevron infrastructure actually needs allocated at the process level and what its lifecycle looks like. If that inventory reveals a distinct pattern, the separation earns its place. If it doesn't, those objects just get their memory from the general pool like everything else.

**On the `MemoryAllocator?` attribute**

This one I'd want to hear more from you on, because right now it's the least defined of the three. Is this intended to be the thing that actually calls `mmap` or `aligned_alloc` — the raw OS interface? If so, that's a thin wrapper around system allocation calls, and the question is whether it warrants being a separate type versus just being a private function inside `ProcessMemoryPool` or `MemoryCore`. A separate type would make sense if you want to swap allocation strategies (maybe `mmap` on Linux, `VirtualAlloc` on Windows) behind a common interface, which given Chevron's cross-platform targets is actually a reasonable motivation.

**Where I'd suggest we land for now**

`MemoryCore` as an orchestrator with `ProcessMemoryPool` as a composed member is justified, provided `MemoryCore` is genuinely doing policy and coordination work that doesn't belong in the pool. The budget ceiling enforcement, the `preallocate` surface, the `acquire`/`release` interface for downstream components, and the event-loop return path integration — those are orchestration concerns that sit above the pool's mechanics.

`ProcessMemoryPool` is the mechanical core — it holds chunks, manages the embedded free list, and performs lock-free allocate and deallocate. It doesn't know about budgets, event loops, or infrastructure memory. It knows about blocks.

The infrastructure memory and the allocator abstraction are both plausible ideas, but I think they need more definition before we commit them as composed members. My suggestion would be: let's converge the design on `ProcessMemoryPool` first since that's the mechanical heart and the thing we've spent this entire conversation understanding. Once that's solid, we can revisit what else `MemoryCore` needs to orchestrate and whether those concerns warrant their own types.

What's your reaction to this?

Conceptually, it sits at the same level as any other downstream component that requests memory from `MemoryCore` — it just happens to be a Chevron-internal consumer rather than a user-code consumer.

If you want `MemoryCore` to be the single point of truth for *all* process-level memory — including knowing what Chevron has reserved for itself — then composing `InfrastructureMemory` inside it is defensible. If you want `MemoryCore` to be purely the acquisition-and-distribution authority with no knowledge of who its consumers are, then `InfrastructureMemory` lives elsewhere.

Good. Let's dig into conflict 2.

**Conflict 2: Deallocation concurrency — CAS push from any thread vs. event-loop single writer**

To argue this one fairly, I need to lay out what each approach actually costs and buys you in concrete terms.

**The case for CAS push from any thread**

Any thread that wants to return a block writes the current head pointer into the block as its next-pointer, then performs a CAS on the head — "if the head is still what I read, swap it to this block." If another thread modified the head between the read and the CAS, it fails and retries.

The advantage is simplicity and immediacy. The block is back in the free list the moment the CAS succeeds. No intermediate queuing, no deferred processing, no dependency on another subsystem being alive and running. The pool is entirely self-contained — it doesn't need to know about event loops or message queues or anything outside itself.

The cost is contention under concurrent deallocation. If many threads are returning blocks simultaneously, the CAS retries increase. Each retry means re-reading the head, re-writing the next-pointer into the block, and trying again. Under heavy concurrent return traffic, this burns CPU cycles on retries. There's also the cache line bouncing — the head pointer lives on a single cache line, and every CAS from any core forces that line to bounce through the cache coherence protocol.

**The case for event-loop single writer**

A thread that wants to return a block doesn't touch the free list at all. It posts a lightweight message (essentially just the block's pointer) onto a queue. The event loop thread, running on its own cadence, drains that queue and pushes the returned blocks onto the free list one at a time. Since only the event loop thread ever writes to the free list head on the return side, there is zero contention on the push path. No CAS, no retries, no cache line bouncing from concurrent pushers.

The cost is latency and dependency. The block isn't available for reallocation until the event loop gets around to processing the return. If the event loop is busy or delayed, returned blocks sit in the queue unavailable. There's also the queue itself — the "cheap queue post" has to be a lock-free multi-producer queue (since any thread can post), so you've moved the CAS contention from the free list to the queue. You haven't eliminated the atomic contention, you've relocated it.

And there's the architectural dependency. `ProcessMemoryPool` would need to either know about the event loop or receive returned blocks exclusively through a channel that the event loop mediates. That means the pool can't function independently — it requires the event loop infrastructure to be running for deallocation to work.

**Where I think the resolution lives**

Here's the key question: does relocating the contention from the free list to the event loop queue actually buy you anything?

In the CAS-on-the-free-list model, a return involves one CAS on the head pointer. In the event-loop model, a return involves one atomic push onto a multi-producer queue (which is itself a CAS or equivalent), plus later the event loop does a non-contended write to the free list head. You've traded one contended CAS for one contended CAS plus one non-contended write. The total work is the same or slightly more.

The event loop model wins if the queue is fundamentally cheaper to push onto than the free list. And it can be — a multi-producer queue can be designed with per-thread submission slots or batched submissions that reduce the CAS frequency. But that's added complexity in the queue design to save complexity on the free list, which is a lateral move in terms of overall system simplicity.

The event loop model also wins if you want the return path to do additional bookkeeping beyond just pushing a block back onto the free list. If the event loop thread, as the single writer, also updates chunk-level free counts, adjusts statistics, or performs any other accounting that would be expensive to do atomically from arbitrary threads, then funneling returns through a single thread is genuinely valuable. The single-writer pattern isn't just about the free list push — it's about everything that happens alongside the push.

**My position**

I think the event-loop return path was the right idea for the *wrong layer*. At the `MemoryCore` level — where `release()` might involve budget accounting, statistics updates, and coordination with the allocator — single-writer semantics through the event loop are genuinely useful. The event loop processes returns and handles all the policy-level bookkeeping that would be expensive to do atomically.

But at the `ProcessMemoryPool` level, the push operation is just a pointer write and a CAS. There's no bookkeeping to protect. Making the pool depend on an external event loop for its most basic operation — returning a block — couples it to infrastructure that has nothing to do with pool mechanics.

So my proposed resolution is: `ProcessMemoryPool` uses CAS for both allocation and deallocation. It is self-contained and has no dependency on the event loop. `MemoryCore`'s `release()` method can still route through the event loop if there's policy-level work to do on the return path, and when the event loop is ready, it calls into the pool's CAS-based deallocation. The pool doesn't know or care that its deallocation was called from an event loop thread — it just does the CAS like it would for anyone.

This gives you the event-loop single-writer benefit where it matters (policy bookkeeping in `MemoryCore`) without burdening `ProcessMemoryPool` with an architectural dependency it doesn't need. The pool stays mechanical and self-contained. `MemoryCore` decides how to use it.

**Why the concern was legitimate**

Picture the scenario you described. A `MemoryScope` three levels deep has 6 siblings, all finishing work around the same time on different threads. All 7 of them try to return memory to their shared parent simultaneously. If the parent's return path involves an atomic CAS on a single free list head, all 7 threads are hammering the same cache line at the same time. Most of those CAS operations fail on the first attempt because another thread modified the head between the read and the swap. Each failure means a retry — re-read the head, re-write the next-pointer, try again. Under heavy concurrent returns, a thread might retry several times before succeeding. The calling thread is spinning on retries instead of doing useful work.

That's a real cost. The event loop idea eliminated it entirely by making returns a queue post — the calling thread drops the block into a queue and moves on immediately. The event loop thread handles the actual free list push later, alone, with zero contention.

So the motivation was sound: protect the calling thread from contention-induced stalls on the return path.

**Why I think CAS is still the right answer**

The concern is about the *magnitude* of the cost, and this is where the specifics matter.

A CAS retry on a modern x86-64 processor takes roughly the time of a cache line roundtrip through the coherence protocol — somewhere in the range of 20 to 80 nanoseconds depending on whether the cores are on the same socket. A successful CAS with no contention is even cheaper. Even in your worst case — 7 siblings all returning simultaneously — the contention window is tiny because the critical section is just a pointer read and a CAS. There's no computation between reading the head and attempting the swap, so the window during which another thread can interfere is as small as it can possibly be. Most threads will succeed on the first or second attempt.

Compare that to the event loop path. The calling thread has to perform an atomic push onto a multi-producer queue — which is itself a CAS or equivalent atomic operation on the queue's internal state. So you haven't eliminated the atomic contention, you've moved it from the free list to the queue. Then you've added latency — the block isn't available for reallocation until the event loop processes it. And you've added an infrastructure dependency — the event loop must be running for returns to work at all.

The event loop wins if the work being deferred is *expensive* — if the return path involves significant bookkeeping that you don't want on the calling thread. But if the return path is just a CAS push onto a free list, the event loop is adding complexity and latency to avoid a cost that's already near the minimum possible.

If we decide CAS-based returns are sufficient at the `ProcessMemoryPool` level, the same reasoning applies at every level of the hierarchy. A `MemoryScope` returning a block to its parent `MemoryScope` would also just CAS-push onto the parent's free list. The calling thread does one atomic operation and moves on. The contention window is the same tiny pointer-swap at every level.

No event loop dependency at any level. No deferred processing. No queue infrastructure. The return path is uniform and self-contained from top to bottom.

Drop the event loop return path for now. Use CAS-based push for returns at every level, including `ProcessMemoryPool`. The contention cost is minimal for the operation size. If profiling later shows a specific level of the hierarchy suffering from return contention, you can introduce batching or event-loop mediation at that level as a targeted optimization. **Conflict 3: Thread memory strategy — per-thread caching with batch transfers vs. geometric thread-local growth**

Let me make sure I'm representing both approaches accurately before we argue them.

**Per-thread caching with batch transfers (from this chat)**

Each thread maintains a small local cache of blocks. When the cache is empty and the thread needs a block, it goes to the shared pool and grabs a batch of blocks in one atomic operation, filling its local cache. Subsequent allocations come from the local cache with no atomics at all. When the cache is full (too many returned blocks accumulating), the thread pushes a batch back to the shared pool in one atomic operation. The batch size is a tuning parameter — larger batches mean fewer trips to the shared pool but more memory sitting idle in local caches.

The key property is that blocks flow back and forth between the thread-local cache and the shared pool. A thread that allocates heavily drains its cache and refills from the pool. A thread that deallocates heavily fills its cache and drains back to the pool. Memory circulates.

**`free_list_head` — atomic pointer to the first available block**

This is the single pointer that the entire allocation and deallocation mechanism revolves around. It points to the first free block in the embedded linked list. That block contains a pointer to the next free block, which contains a pointer to the next, and so on until a null pointer marks the end of the chain.

Every allocation reads this pointer, follows it one hop to the next free block, and CAS-swaps the head to point to that next block. Every deallocation writes the current head into the returned block and CAS-swaps the head to point to the returned block. This is the only shared mutable state that the allocation and deallocation paths touch.

It must be atomic because multiple threads may allocate or deallocate concurrently. The CAS operations on this pointer are the synchronization mechanism for the entire pool. On x86-64, an atomic pointer is 8 bytes and the CAS is a single `lock cmpxchg` instruction.

One consideration we discussed — the ABA problem. A thread reads the head, gets preempted, another thread allocates and then deallocates the same block back to the head, and the first thread's CAS succeeds even though the list changed underneath. We talked about tagged pointers as the classic solution — pairing the pointer with a monotonically increasing counter so the CAS checks both values. If we go that route, this attribute wouldn't be a plain atomic pointer but an atomic pair of pointer and counter, which on x86-64 fits in a 16-byte compare-and-swap (`lock cmpxchg16b`). Whether we need this depends on how likely ABA is given your usage patterns — at the process pool level with infrequent large-block operations, it may be a non-issue, but for a general-purpose library where you can't predict usage, the tagged pointer is the safer choice.

Good call on zero ABA tolerance. Let me address the platform question first because it has real implications.

---

**The 16-byte CAS across platforms**

On x86-64, `lock cmpxchg16b` is a single instruction that atomically compares and swaps 16 bytes. It's widely supported — essentially every x86-64 processor from the last 15 years has it. The cost is comparable to a regular 8-byte CAS, maybe slightly higher due to the wider bus operation, but it's a solved problem on this architecture.

On ARM64 (which matters for macOS on Apple Silicon and potentially Linux on ARM servers), there is no single 16-byte CAS instruction. ARM64 uses a load-exclusive/store-exclusive pair (`ldxp`/`stxp`) that can operate on a pair of 8-byte registers, giving you 16-byte atomics. The behavior is correct but the performance characteristics are different — under contention, the exclusive monitor can be cleared by other cores more aggressively than x86's cache line locking, which means more retries. In practice for low-contention scenarios like your process-level pool, this is unlikely to be measurable.

The real concern is `std::atomic` support. The C++ standard doesn't guarantee that `std::atomic<T>` is lock-free for any particular size of T. You can check at compile time with `std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free`, or at runtime with the `is_lock_free()` member. For 16-byte types, most major compilers on x86-64 and ARM64 do provide lock-free atomics, but it's not universal. On a platform where 16-byte atomics are *not* lock-free, the implementation falls back to a mutex internally — which defeats the entire point of your lock-free design.

**How to handle this robustly**

You have two options.

The first is to use a 16-byte atomic struct — a pointer and a `uint64_t` counter packed together — and `static_assert` that it's lock-free at compile time. If someone tries to build Chevron on a platform where 16-byte atomics aren't lock-free, the build fails with a clear message rather than silently falling back to a mutex. This is the strictest approach and it guarantees your performance promise.

The second option is to fit the tag into the pointer itself, keeping the whole thing at 8 bytes. On x86-64, virtual addresses currently only use 48 bits of the 64-bit pointer (the upper 16 bits are sign-extended). You can pack a 16-bit generation counter into those upper bits, mask it out when you need the actual address, and do your CAS on a plain 8-byte atomic. This is called pointer tagging or pointer packing. It gives you lock-free 8-byte CAS on every platform that supports 8-byte atomics, which is effectively all of them.

The tradeoff is that the 16-bit counter wraps at 65536. For ABA to occur, a block would have to be allocated, freed, and returned to the exact same head position 65536 times between another thread's read and CAS — which is practically impossible at your pool's operation frequency. But it's theoretically imperfect, whereas the full 64-bit counter in the 16-byte approach effectively never wraps.

There's also a portability subtlety with pointer tagging. The assumption that upper bits are unused is architecture-specific. ARM64 has Top Byte Ignore (TBI) which gives you 8 bits to play with. Future x86 extensions (like Linear Address Masking) may change the available bits. You'd need to abstract the tag manipulation behind a platform-aware utility so that the bit layout adapts per target.

**My recommendation**

For a cross-platform library, the 16-byte atomic with a compile-time lock-free assertion is the cleaner approach. It's explicit, portable, and doesn't depend on architecture-specific pointer layout assumptions. Every platform Chevron targets (x86-64 Linux and Windows, ARM64 macOS) supports lock-free 16-byte atomics in practice. The `static_assert` catches any future platform where that isn't true, and you deal with it then rather than discovering a silent performance regression.

**On your point about the counter serving additional purposes**

Good instinct. Since you're paying for a 64-bit counter anyway, it can serve as more than just an ABA guard. It's a monotonically increasing operation counter on the free list — every push or pop increments it. That gives you a total operation count for free, which is useful for diagnostics and statistics. You could split it into two 32-bit counters if you wanted — one for allocations, one for deallocations — and the difference between them tells you how many blocks are currently outstanding. That's a live utilization metric with zero additional bookkeeping cost, derived entirely from a value you're already maintaining for correctness.

Whether you want to commit to that split now or keep it as a single 64-bit generation counter is up to you. The single counter is simpler and maximizes the ABA protection range. The split counter gives you richer diagnostics but wraps sooner on each half.

**`chunk_descriptors` — the fixed array tracking acquired chunks**

We established that the pool needs to know which chunks it owns so it can release them all at destruction. We also established that the maximum number of chunks is known at construction time — the memory ceiling divided by the chunk size gives you the upper bound on how many chunks the pool will ever hold.

This means we can allocate a fixed-size array at construction and never grow it. Each entry in the array needs to record two things: the base pointer of the chunk (the address returned by the allocator, which is what you pass back when releasing) and the size of the chunk. Together those two values are enough to describe the chunk for both cleanup and for any validation you might want to do later.

You already have a type for this — `MemoryRegion`, the lightweight value type carrying a base pointer and size. So each entry in the chunk descriptor array is a `MemoryRegion`. The array itself could be a `std::array` if the maximum count is a compile-time constant, or a heap-allocated fixed buffer if the maximum is determined at construction from the runtime ceiling and chunk size parameters. Given that the ceiling and chunk size are construction-time parameters rather than compile-time constants, a heap-allocated buffer sized once at construction is the natural fit.

There's a nuance here though. The pool acquires chunks lazily — it doesn't fill all the way to the ceiling at construction. So the array has a capacity (the maximum number of chunks) and a count (how many have actually been acquired so far). That count increases as the pool grows and never decreases, since we don't return memory to the OS during runtime.

**`chunk_count` — how many chunks have been acquired**

A `std::size_t` that starts at zero and increments each time the pool acquires a new chunk from the allocator. Combined with the chunk descriptor array, it tells you which entries are valid. Entries from index 0 through `chunk_count - 1` describe real acquired chunks. Entries from `chunk_count` onward are unused slots.

This value is written when the pool grows (a new chunk is acquired) and read during destruction (to know how many chunks to release). The growth path needs consideration for thread safety — if two threads exhaust the free list simultaneously and both try to trigger growth, only one should actually acquire a new chunk. But growth is a slow path that we'll address when we discuss operations. For now, this is the counter that tracks it.

**`max_chunk_count` — the capacity of the descriptor array**

Derived at construction from the ceiling and chunk size. Stored so that the growth path can check "have we hit the ceiling" without recomputing it. A simple `std::size_t`, constant after construction.

Now — there's a question here about the relationship between `ProcessMemoryPool` and `MemoryAllocator`. The chunk descriptor array tracks what has been acquired, but the pool itself doesn't acquire chunks — `MemoryAllocator` does. When the pool needs to grow, who initiates that? Does the pool call into the allocator directly, or does it signal `MemoryCore` that it needs more memory and `MemoryCore` orchestrates the acquisition?

This matters because it affects what the pool holds a reference to. If the pool calls the allocator directly, it needs a reference or pointer to the `MemoryAllocator`. If it signals upward and receives chunks from above, it stays fully decoupled from the allocation mechanism and just has a "here's a new chunk, add it" operation.

Here's my honest take.

Separating the allocator made sense as a concept — isolating the platform-specific OS calls behind a clean interface so the pool doesn't know whether it's calling `mmap` or `VirtualAlloc` or `aligned_alloc`. That's a real concern for a cross-platform library. The abstraction isn't wrong in principle.

But here's the practical reality. The pool is the only consumer of that allocator. Nobody else in the system acquires raw chunks from the OS. `MemoryCore` doesn't. `MemoryScope` doesn't. `InfrastructureMemory` doesn't — it gets blocks from the pool like everyone else. The allocator exists to serve exactly one client, and that client is `ProcessMemoryPool`.

When you have a type whose sole reason to exist is to serve one other type, and that type is composed directly inside the thing it serves, you have to ask what the separation is buying you. The answer is: a clean compile-time boundary between platform-specific allocation calls and pool mechanics. That's a legitimate benefit, but you can achieve the same thing with a private method or a small platform-abstraction header without elevating it to a full composed type with its own identity and lifecycle.

The risk of separating them is exactly what you ran into — the interaction between the pool and the allocator becomes an interface design problem. Who calls whom, who holds a reference to whom, what happens during growth, what happens during cleanup. These are questions that only exist because you split something that has a single natural owner and a single consumer.

Collapsing them is the right call. Put the OS acquisition logic inside `ProcessMemoryPool` as private implementation detail. If you want platform isolation, a private method like `acquire_chunk_from_os(std::size_t size, std::size_t alignment)` that you implement per platform behind `#ifdef` blocks or a platform header gives you the same separation without the architectural overhead. If you later discover a genuine second consumer of raw OS memory — which I doubt will happen — you can extract the allocator at that point with a clear motivation.

So no, you're not overreacting. You identified a premature abstraction and collapsed it. That's good engineering judgment. The pool acquires its own memory, tracks its own chunks, manages its own free list. One class, one responsibility, no unnecessary indirection.

This also simplifies `MemoryCore`. It now composes one member — `ProcessMemoryPool` — and provides the policy surface (`acquire`, `release`, budget enforcement, `preallocate`) on top of it. Clean and focused.

Actually — let me stop here. This one raises the question of whether the budget ceiling belongs in `ProcessMemoryPool` or in `MemoryCore`. We said `MemoryCore` is the policy layer and the pool is the mechanical layer. The ceiling is a policy constraint — "you may not acquire more than X bytes total." The pool mechanically acquires chunks and manages blocks. The ceiling limits how many chunks the pool is allowed to acquire.

There are two ways to handle this. Either the pool holds the ceiling and enforces it internally during growth, or `MemoryCore` holds the ceiling and the pool has no concept of a maximum — it just acquires chunks when told to, and `MemoryCore` is the one that decides whether to tell it to grow or to throw `bad_alloc`.

If the pool enforces its own ceiling, it's self-contained — it can never overrun regardless of what `MemoryCore` does. But it's making a policy decision, which we said belongs in `MemoryCore`.

If `MemoryCore` enforces the ceiling, the pool is purely mechanical — "give me a chunk" always works until the OS refuses. But then a bug in `MemoryCore` could allow the pool to grow past the intended budget.

My lean is that the pool should hold the ceiling and enforce it, even though it's technically a policy concern. The consequence of exceeding the ceiling is severe enough — unbounded memory growth in a library that promises a hard cap — that defense in depth justifies putting the check at the lowest level. `MemoryCore` can also enforce it at the policy layer, and the pool's internal check serves as a safety net.

**Thread-local state — the geometric growth caches**

This is where the per-thread contention reduction lives. Each thread that interacts with the pool gets its own local cache of blocks. The first time a thread needs a block, it goes to the shared free list and grabs a small initial batch. When that local cache is exhausted, it goes back to the shared free list and grabs double what it grabbed last time. Each subsequent trip doubles again.

The thread-local state needs to hold three things per thread.

A local free list — the thread's private stash of blocks. This could be as simple as a pointer to the head of a small singly-linked list using the same embedded next-pointer scheme as the shared free list. No atomics needed here because only the owning thread ever touches it.

A current batch size — how many blocks this thread grabbed on its last trip to the shared pool. Starts at some reasonable initial value and doubles each time. This is what makes the growth geometric.

A maximum batch size — a cap on how large the geometric growth can get, preventing a single thread from claiming an unreasonable share of the pool in one trip. Without this, a long-lived thread that keeps exhausting its cache would eventually try to grab half the pool in a single batch.

The mechanism for associating this state with a thread is `thread_local` storage. A `thread_local` struct holding the local free list head, the current batch size, and the max batch size. When a thread first accesses the pool, the struct is initialized with an empty local free list and the initial batch size.

Doing 16 individual CAS operations to fill a batch of 16 defeats much of the purpose — you've just done 16 contended atomics instead of one. The alternative is to walk the free list from the current head to find the Nth block, then CAS-swap the head to the block after the Nth — effectively popping N blocks in a single CAS. This only works if no other thread modifies the list between your traversal and your CAS, which under contention isn't guaranteed, so you'd retry. But the expected case is that one traversal plus one CAS transfers an entire batch, which is dramatically better than N individual pops.

The same logic applies in reverse when a thread wants to return a batch — link the blocks together locally, then CAS the last block's next-pointer to the current head and swap the head to the first block in the batch. One CAS to push N blocks.

This is the mechanical core of the contention reduction. The shared free list is only touched when a thread's local cache is empty or needs to drain, and each touch transfers multiple blocks.

Do you want these to be construction-time parameters on the pool, or compile-time constants, or something else? 1	---
     2	name: docx
     3	description: "Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation."
     4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     5	---
     6	
     7	# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis
     8	
     9	## Overview
    10	
    11	A .docx file is a ZIP archive containing XML files.
    12	
    13	## Quick Reference
    14	
    15	| Task | Approach |
    16	|------|----------|
    17	| Read/analyze content | `pandoc` or unpack for raw XML |
    18	| Create new document | Use `docx-js` - see Creating New Documents below |
    19	| Edit existing document | Unpack → edit XML → repack - see Editing Existing Documents below |
    20	
    21	### Converting .doc to .docx
    22	
    23	Legacy `.doc` files must be converted before editing:
    24	
    25	```bash
    26	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx document.doc
    27	```
    28	
    29	### Reading Content
    30	
    31	```bash
    32	# Text extraction with tracked changes
    33	pandoc --track-changes=all document.docx -o output.md
    34	
    35	# Raw XML access
    36	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
    37	```
    38	
    39	### Converting to Images
    40	
    41	```bash
    42	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf document.docx
    43	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 document.pdf page
    44	```
    45	
    46	### Accepting Tracked Changes
    47	
    48	To produce a clean document with all tracked changes accepted (requires LibreOffice):
    49	
    50	```bash
    51	python scripts/accept_changes.py input.docx output.docx
    52	```
    53	
    54	---
    55	
    56	## Creating New Documents
    57	
    58	Generate .docx files with JavaScript, then validate. Install: `npm install -g docx`
    59	
    60	### Setup
    61	```javascript
    62	const { Document, Packer, Paragraph, TextRun, Table, TableRow, TableCell, ImageRun,
    63	        Header, Footer, AlignmentType, PageOrientation, LevelFormat, ExternalHyperlink,
    64	        InternalHyperlink, Bookmark, FootnoteReferenceRun, PositionalTab,
    65	        PositionalTabAlignment, PositionalTabRelativeTo, PositionalTabLeader,
    66	        TabStopType, TabStopPosition, Column, SectionType,
    67	        TableOfContents, HeadingLevel, BorderStyle, WidthType, ShadingType,
    68	        VerticalAlign, PageNumber, PageBreak } = require('docx');
    69	
    70	const doc = new Document({ sections: [{ children: [/* content */] }] });
    71	Packer.toBuffer(doc).then(buffer => fs.writeFileSync("doc.docx", buffer));
    72	```
    73	
    74	### Validation
    75	After creating the file, validate it. If validation fails, unpack, fix the XML, and repack.
    76	```bash
    77	python scripts/office/validate.py doc.docx
    78	```
    79	
    80	### Page Size
    81	
    82	```javascript
    83	// CRITICAL: docx-js defaults to A4, not US Letter
    84	// Always set page size explicitly for consistent results
    85	sections: [{
    86	  properties: {
    87	    page: {
    88	      size: {
    89	        width: 12240,   // 8.5 inches in DXA
    90	        height: 15840   // 11 inches in DXA
    91	      },
    92	      margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 } // 1 inch margins
    93	    }
    94	  },
    95	  children: [/* content */]
    96	}]
    97	```
    98	
    99	**Common page sizes (DXA units, 1440 DXA = 1 inch):**
   100	
   101	| Paper | Width | Height | Content Width (1" margins) |
   102	|-------|-------|--------|---------------------------|
   103	| US Letter | 12,240 | 15,840 | 9,360 |
   104	| A4 (default) | 11,906 | 16,838 | 9,026 |
   105	
   106	**Landscape orientation:** docx-js swaps width/height internally, so pass portrait dimensions and let it handle the swap:
   107	```javascript
   108	size: {
   109	  width: 12240,   // Pass SHORT edge as width
   110	  height: 15840,  // Pass LONG edge as height
   111	  orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE  // docx-js swaps them in the XML
   112	},
   113	// Content width = 15840 - left margin - right margin (uses the long edge)
   114	```
   115	
   116	### Styles (Override Built-in Headings)
   117	
   118	Use Arial as the default font (universally supported). Keep titles black for readability.
   119	
   120	```javascript
   121	const doc = new Document({
   122	  styles: {
   123	    default: { document: { run: { font: "Arial", size: 24 } } }, // 12pt default
   124	    paragraphStyles: [
   125	      // IMPORTANT: Use exact IDs to override built-in styles
   126	      { id: "Heading1", name: "Heading 1", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   127	        run: { size: 32, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   128	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 240, after: 240 }, outlineLevel: 0 } }, // outlineLevel required for TOC
   129	      { id: "Heading2", name: "Heading 2", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   130	        run: { size: 28, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   131	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 180, after: 180 }, outlineLevel: 1 } },
   132	    ]
   133	  },
   134	  sections: [{
   135	    children: [
   136	      new Paragraph({ heading: HeadingLevel.HEADING_1, children: [new TextRun("Title")] }),
   137	    ]
   138	  }]
   139	});
   140	```
   141	
   142	### Lists (NEVER use unicode bullets)
   143	
   144	```javascript
   145	// ❌ WRONG - never manually insert bullet characters
   146	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("• Item")] })  // BAD
   147	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("\u2022 Item")] })  // BAD
   148	
   149	// ✅ CORRECT - use numbering config with LevelFormat.BULLET
   150	const doc = new Document({
   151	  numbering: {
   152	    config: [
   153	      { reference: "bullets",
   154	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.BULLET, text: "•", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   155	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   156	      { reference: "numbers",
   157	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.DECIMAL, text: "%1.", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   158	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   159	    ]
   160	  },
   161	  sections: [{
   162	    children: [
   163	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "bullets", level: 0 },
   164	        children: [new TextRun("Bullet item")] }),
   165	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "numbers", level: 0 },
   166	        children: [new TextRun("Numbered item")] }),
   167	    ]
   168	  }]
   169	});
   170	
   171	// ⚠️ Each reference creates INDEPENDENT numbering
   172	// Same reference = continues (1,2,3 then 4,5,6)
   173	// Different reference = restarts (1,2,3 then 1,2,3)
   174	```
   175	
   176	### Tables
   177	
   178	**CRITICAL: Tables need dual widths** - set both `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on each cell. Without both, tables render incorrectly on some platforms.
   179	
   180	```javascript
   181	// CRITICAL: Always set table width for consistent rendering
   182	// CRITICAL: Use ShadingType.CLEAR (not SOLID) to prevent black backgrounds
   183	const border = { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 1, color: "CCCCCC" };
   184	const borders = { top: border, bottom: border, left: border, right: border };
   185	
   186	new Table({
   187	  width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Always use DXA (percentages break in Google Docs)
   188	  columnWidths: [4680, 4680], // Must sum to table width (DXA: 1440 = 1 inch)
   189	  rows: [
   190	    new TableRow({
   191	      children: [
   192	        new TableCell({
   193	          borders,
   194	          width: { size: 4680, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Also set on each cell
   195	          shading: { fill: "D5E8F0", type: ShadingType.CLEAR }, // CLEAR not SOLID
   196	          margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }, // Cell padding (internal, not added to width)
   197	          children: [new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("Cell")] })]
   198	        })
   199	      ]
   200	    })
   201	  ]
   202	})
   203	```
   204	
   205	**Table width calculation:**
   206	
   207	Always use `WidthType.DXA` — `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` breaks in Google Docs.
   208	
   209	```javascript
   210	// Table width = sum of columnWidths = content width
   211	// US Letter with 1" margins: 12240 - 2880 = 9360 DXA
   212	width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA },
   213	columnWidths: [7000, 2360]  // Must sum to table width
   214	```
   215	
   216	**Width rules:**
	< truncated lines 217-374 >
   375	}]
   376	```
   377	
   378	### Critical Rules for docx-js
   379	
   380	- **Set page size explicitly** - docx-js defaults to A4; use US Letter (12240 x 15840 DXA) for US documents
   381	- **Landscape: pass portrait dimensions** - docx-js swaps width/height internally; pass short edge as `width`, long edge as `height`, and set `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE`
   382	- **Never use `\n`** - use separate Paragraph elements
   383	- **Never use unicode bullets** - use `LevelFormat.BULLET` with numbering config
   384	- **PageBreak must be in Paragraph** - standalone creates invalid XML
   385	- **ImageRun requires `type`** - always specify png/jpg/etc
   386	- **Always set table `width` with DXA** - never use `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` (breaks in Google Docs)
   387	- **Tables need dual widths** - `columnWidths` array AND cell `width`, both must match
   388	- **Table width = sum of columnWidths** - for DXA, ensure they add up exactly
   389	- **Always add cell margins** - use `margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }` for readable padding
   390	- **Use `ShadingType.CLEAR`** - never SOLID for table shading
   391	- **Never use tables as dividers/rules** - cells have minimum height and render as empty boxes (including in headers/footers); use `border: { bottom: { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 6, color: "2E75B6", space: 1 } }` on a Paragraph instead. For two-column footers, use tab stops (see Tab Stops section), not tables
   392	- **TOC requires HeadingLevel only** - no custom styles on heading paragraphs
   393	- **Override built-in styles** - use exact IDs: "Heading1", "Heading2", etc.
   394	- **Include `outlineLevel`** - required for TOC (0 for H1, 1 for H2, etc.)
   395	
   396	---
   397	
   398	## Editing Existing Documents
   399	
   400	**Follow all 3 steps in order.**
   401	
   402	### Step 1: Unpack
   403	```bash
   404	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
   405	```
   406	Extracts XML, pretty-prints, merges adjacent runs, and converts smart quotes to XML entities (`“` etc.) so they survive editing. Use `--merge-runs false` to skip run merging.
   407	
   408	### Step 2: Edit XML
   409	
   410	Edit files in `unpacked/word/`. See XML Reference below for patterns.
   411	
   412	**Use "Claude" as the author** for tracked changes and comments, unless the user explicitly requests use of a different name.
   413	
   414	**Use the Edit tool directly for string replacement. Do not write Python scripts.** Scripts introduce unnecessary complexity. The Edit tool shows exactly what is being replaced.
   415	
   416	**CRITICAL: Use smart quotes for new content.** When adding text with apostrophes or quotes, use XML entities to produce smart quotes:
   417	```xml
   418	<!-- Use these entities for professional typography -->
   419	<w:t>Here’s a quote: “Hello”</w:t>
   420	```
   421	| Entity | Character |
   422	|--------|-----------|
   423	| `‘` | ‘ (left single) |
   424	| `’` | ’ (right single / apostrophe) |
   425	| `“` | “ (left double) |
   426	| `”` | ” (right double) |
   427	
   428	**Adding comments:** Use `comment.py` to handle boilerplate across multiple XML files (text must be pre-escaped XML):
   429	```bash
   430	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Comment text with & and ’"
   431	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 1 "Reply text" --parent 0  # reply to comment 0
   432	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Text" --author "Custom Author"  # custom author name
   433	```
   434	Then add markers to document.xml (see Comments in XML Reference).
   435	
   436	### Step 3: Pack
   437	```bash
   438	python scripts/office/pack.py unpacked/ output.docx --original document.docx
   439	```
   440	Validates with auto-repair, condenses XML, and creates DOCX. Use `--validate false` to skip.
   441	
   442	**Auto-repair will fix:**
   443	- `durableId` >= 0x7FFFFFFF (regenerates valid ID)
   444	- Missing `xml:space="preserve"` on `<w:t>` with whitespace
   445	
   446	**Auto-repair won't fix:**
   447	- Malformed XML, invalid element nesting, missing relationships, schema violations
   448	
   449	### Common Pitfalls
   450	
   451	- **Replace entire `<w:r>` elements**: When adding tracked changes, replace the whole `<w:r>...</w:r>` block with `<w:del>...<w:ins>...` as siblings. Don't inject tracked change tags inside a run.
   452	- **Preserve `<w:rPr>` formatting**: Copy the original run's `<w:rPr>` block into your tracked change runs to maintain bold, font size, etc.
   453	
   454	---
   455	
   456	## XML Reference
   457	
   458	### Schema Compliance
   459	
   460	- **Element order in `<w:pPr>`**: `<w:pStyle>`, `<w:numPr>`, `<w:spacing>`, `<w:ind>`, `<w:jc>`, `<w:rPr>` last
   461	- **Whitespace**: Add `xml:space="preserve"` to `<w:t>` with leading/trailing spaces
   462	- **RSIDs**: Must be 8-digit hex (e.g., `00AB1234`)
   463	
   464	### Tracked Changes
   465	
   466	**Insertion:**
   467	```xml
   468	<w:ins w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   469	  <w:r><w:t>inserted text</w:t></w:r>
   470	</w:ins>
   471	```
   472	
   473	**Deletion:**
   474	```xml
   475	<w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   476	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   477	</w:del>
   478	```
   479	
   480	**Inside `<w:del>`**: Use `<w:delText>` instead of `<w:t>`, and `<w:delInstrText>` instead of `<w:instrText>`.
   481	
   482	**Minimal edits** - only mark what changes:
   483	```xml
   484	<!-- Change "30 days" to "60 days" -->
   485	<w:r><w:t>The term is </w:t></w:r>
   486	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   487	  <w:r><w:delText>30</w:delText></w:r>
   488	</w:del>
   489	<w:ins w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   490	  <w:r><w:t>60</w:t></w:r>
   491	</w:ins>
   492	<w:r><w:t> days.</w:t></w:r>
   493	```
   494	
   495	**Deleting entire paragraphs/list items** - when removing ALL content from a paragraph, also mark the paragraph mark as deleted so it merges with the next paragraph. Add `<w:del/>` inside `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`:
   496	```xml
   497	<w:p>
   498	  <w:pPr>
   499	    <w:numPr>...</w:numPr>  <!-- list numbering if present -->
   500	    <w:rPr>
   501	      <w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>
   502	    </w:rPr>
   503	  </w:pPr>
   504	  <w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   505	    <w:r><w:delText>Entire paragraph content being deleted...</w:delText></w:r>
   506	  </w:del>
   507	</w:p>
   508	```
   509	Without the `<w:del/>` in `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`, accepting changes leaves an empty paragraph/list item.
   510	
   511	**Rejecting another author's insertion** - nest deletion inside their insertion:
   512	```xml
   513	<w:ins w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   514	  <w:del w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   515	    <w:r><w:delText>their inserted text</w:delText></w:r>
   516	  </w:del>
   517	</w:ins>
   518	```
   519	
   520	**Restoring another author's deletion** - add insertion after (don't modify their deletion):
   521	```xml
   522	<w:del w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   523	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   524	</w:del>
   525	<w:ins w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   526	  <w:r><w:t>deleted text</w:t></w:r>
   527	</w:ins>
   528	```
   529	
   530	### Comments
   531	
   532	After running `comment.py` (see Step 2), add markers to document.xml. For replies, use `--parent` flag and nest markers inside the parent's.
   533	
   534	**CRITICAL: `<w:commentRangeStart>` and `<w:commentRangeEnd>` are siblings of `<w:r>`, never inside `<w:r>`.**
   535	
   536	```xml
   537	<!-- Comment markers are direct children of w:p, never inside w:r -->
   538	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   539	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   540	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted</w:delText></w:r>
   541	</w:del>
   542	<w:r><w:t> more text</w:t></w:r>
   543	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   544	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   545	
   546	<!-- Comment 0 with reply 1 nested inside -->
   547	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   548	  <w:commentRangeStart w:id="1"/>
   549	  <w:r><w:t>text</w:t></w:r>
